review_method.pair_rule: Either directed shared-corner fraction strictly exceeds 3/5. Both fractions are recorded. Rows count from 1 under the sheet header.

pairs.reason: The iron barracks has intersecting pitched roofs over the entry. The industrial hall presents one low, lengthwise roof monitor and a long eave.
The pitched roof and projecting gable give way to a tall, squared barrack block with a broad parapet and recessed roof panels.
The industrial hall stretches under a low shed roof. The future hall rises behind a deep parapet, with transverse slots plainly visible from above.
The central dome, stairs and bathing annex keep the same proportions. The industrial vent changes the left edge while the rest of the dome outline repeats.
The round chamber, stair and low surrounding rooms repeat. The changed cap over the side room is too small to give the future bathhouse a distinct profile.
The stack becomes a short capped vent. Both baths still read as one dome and the same low square annex on the same platform.
The classical smithy has two pitched volumes with distinct gables. The industrial smithy has a long, level workshop roof and a projecting stack.
The clustered gables and pointed corner turret give way to a single long nave with a substantial square lantern. The buttresses keep the cathedral legible.
The medieval pointed turret and high roof planes give way to an open, sweeping pair of ribs above the nave and its buttresses.
The industrial cathedral has a low roof with a box lantern. The future cathedral frames the roof with tall curved structural ribs.
Both mine compounds show the same tall framed shaft and gabled side house. The change in headframe cap leaves their main outline nearly intact.
The same rows, pair of upright silos and low end shed dominate both farms. The shed's roof tip is too small to distinguish the eras.
The front wing shortens, but both guildhalls still read as the same main gable with an attached little cross-gable. The added roof pipe carries little weight.
The early library has a broad low roof and rounded end turret. The later reading hall is taller and has a long rectangular roof monitor.
The spreading low roof and rounded turret give way to a tall square archive with a stepped cap over the entry.
The monastery repeats its four-sided cloister and entry gable. The opposite corner towers exchange caps, with little change to the dominant mass.
The medieval cloister ends in two pointed roofs. The future cloister lifts a broad drum and dome over one corner, changing the skyline in both views.
The industrial cloister shows exposed straight roof monitors and a small corner lantern. The future cloister has a broad rounded dome spanning the corner wing.
The observatory's tall slotted half-dome, base and entry project to the same outline. A minor change to one aperture is hard to see at 64 pixels.
The slotted half-dome, nearly cylindrical drum and entry occupy the same outline. The extra panel below the shutter does little for the future era.
Both views repeat the slotted upright observatory and small projecting entry. The shutter panel and a small side attachment are the only apparent changes.
The pump beam, angled legs and tank cluster repeat in both oil wells. The future caps make a small change at the edge of the same equipment.
Both print shops have a single squat box with the same flat roof and front machinery. The added pipe leaves the industrial roof mass nearly identical.
The low, single roof on the early print shop becomes a tall stepped stack above the print room. The front press remains recognizable.
The industrial print shop's low broad roof and single chimney become a high, square, terraced roof over the same print-room entrance.
The industrial station has a large rounded shed next to the ticket house. The future station spreads a flat platform canopy under exposed roof supports.
Both labs carry the same pair of vertical tanks beside a box with the same entry. The roof hatch changes, but the lab's massing and equipment repeat.
Both scriptoria read as the same long room under one plain pitched roof. A short chimney rises in the later version.
The long low writing hall and identical end bays remain dominant. A narrow roof strip produces little change at thumbnail size.
Both scriptoria have the same long, single-storey block, door and slight roof pitch. The future roof seam only affects a few pixels.
The same long low hall exchanges a little chimney for a ridge strip. The entrance, roof span and footprint still read alike.
The long writing hall carries nearly the same low roof, with the older chimney replaced by a thin raised edge.
Both buildings show a thin strip running along the same long roof above identical low writing rooms. The end of that strip changes slightly.
The open shrine keeps its raised altar and steps while the pitched canopy becomes a distinct hemisphere resting on a square cornice.
Both shrines retain the pitched canopy, altar and stepped plinth. Thickening the side supports leaves their silhouettes almost identical.
The open, overhanging temple canopy becomes an enclosed, tall pointed frame surrounding the altar. The steps and shrine remain legible.
The domed classical canopy becomes a clear gabled, overhanging roof above the altar and stair.
The classical round canopy and projecting cornice give way to a tall pointed wall that frames the altar and closes its sides.
The industrial altar sits under a projecting gable roof. The future shrine encloses the same altar between tall sloping sidewalls.
The ancient quarry rises to a roofed stand above its cut. The later quarry has a long low working ledge with open equipment over the rock.
The ancient roofed lookout dominates the quarry skyline. The industrial cut carries an open horizontal gantry on piers with room visible below.
The two quarries carry nearly the same working ledges, rocks and aligned back frame. The industrial equipment reads as a slight extension of that frame.
The stepped stone cut and its horizontal gantry retain the same support arrangement and skyline. The future end cap is too small to differentiate it.
Both temples retain one unbroken pitched roof, the same plinth and nearly identical porch. The rearranged entry posts are hard to separate at 64 pixels.
Both armories are squat stone halls with identical projecting ends. The narrow raised ridge follows the same outline in both views.
The continuous cap becomes a small roof panel, but the armory's thick end supports, doors and slab roof retain the same silhouette.
The future inset on the roof leaves the same long, low armory body and projecting eaves visible.
A short inset vent replaces the long cap. The armory's roof span, bulky shoulders and end bays repeat.
The change is confined to a strip on top of the same slab-roof armory. The silhouette and equipment do not separate the eras.
Both armories carry nearly identical compact roof panels, side ribs and projecting ends on the same wide plinth.
The classical bath hall carries a low hemisphere. A conspicuous pair of tall exhaust stacks rises above the industrial bath hall; its exterior basins preserve its function.
The classical bathhouse terminates in a distinctly round dome. The future hall instead carries a broad rectangular monitor extending over the roof above the same pools.
Two tall, thin stacks above the industrial bath become a low, broad rectangular roof monitor on the future bath. The outer basins remain readable.
The same broad overhanging roof, porch and boat-shaped gear occupy both fishing huts. Only the roof edges change.
Both fishing huts have a single square roof and identical waterside equipment. The slightly flatter roof rim leaves the silhouette essentially intact.
The hut, overhang and boat repeat. The altered roof edge does not visibly change the fishing operation or the era.
The projecting rectangular hut roof still sits above the same boat and dock. The little lip along the roof is the only apparent change.
Both are the same bulky hut with a short dock and adjoining boat. The roof corners flatten slightly.
The roof, dock and boat have essentially the same outlines in each view. The tiny changes at the eaves do not establish a later building.
Above the ore terraces the early mine has a short, studded cap. The classical mine spans the rear with a wide beam carried on upright piers.
The earlier ore workings end in a short rough cap. A conspicuous enclosed rectangular head structure rises above the industrial terraces.
The early mine has a small roofed head assembly. The future workings lift a large crescent of uprights around the head above the stepped cut.
The classical mine crowns its terraces with a straight lintel between uprights. The future machinery has an open round profile enclosed by two curved supports.
A solid, horizontal rectangular head enclosure gives way to an open crescent of equipment on top of the mine terraces.
The medieval hall has a wide, low cap with pitched sides. The industrial hall stacks square tiers into a taller tower over the same buttressed guild floor.
The early guildhall has one broad, low cap. The later tower steps through several narrower tiers above the same square hall.
The classical harbor has a tall open sail-like frame above its quay. The industrial harbor replaces that rig with a squat capped vessel and an open loading frame.
The tall triangular rig and single quay house become a low working vessel alongside a bulky, capped loading structure over the same quay.
The industrial quay has a tall open portal with a small pointed fitting on the adjacent craft. The future quay has a squat rectangular hood and a denser loading assembly.
Both lodges repeat a low slab-roof hall with an identical rack projecting past its end. The slight change to the door framing is invisible in the outline.
Both farms have the same long, pitched growing shed in front and a second roof behind. The rear roof ribs and chimney cap make a small change.
The early market sits under a broad hipped roof. The classical stalls have a flatter projecting eave and a distinct second raised tier.
The early market has one broad sloping roof. The industrial market's two separate raised roofs break the outline above a long stall canopy.
One unbroken hipped roof over the iron market gives way to a raised central lantern and a flat outer canopy over the stalls.
One broad, central raised cap above the classical market changes into two clearly separated rectangular roof volumes above the industrial stalls.
Both markets have a central, low raised cap and the same surrounding eave. Changing the small cap profile does little to distinguish the future stalls.
The industrial market shows two clearly separated roof bays. A single centered lantern rises over the same stall canopy in the future market.
The same mine headframe, cross braces and ore at its feet dominate both models. The older frame is slightly shorter and wider.
Both mines have a roofed, splayed headframe on a mound with the same bins. The industrial cap widens, but the outline and operation repeat.
The same four-legged frame and bins stand over the pit. A small raised roof tile appears at its summit in the future version.
The classical and industrial mines have the same tall tapered headframe and bin arrangement. The larger flat cap is a small skyline change.
The roofed headframe and front bins match in both views. The future cap gains a little rectangular step.
The industrial and future mine frames trace the same tall tapered outline. The small inset on top of the headframe does not distinguish its era.
The industrial station reads as an open-sided shed beside the track with a narrow upright. The future station builds a taller, solid stepped block over the platform.
The same chunky square temple, broad roof, central fixture and projecting front repeat. The front steps are the only appreciable change.
Both temples have the same broad roof, tiny central ridge, entry and side supports. The industrial front panel changes little at 64 pixels.
The iron and future temples show the same low canopy and central roof fitting above a projecting front. The outline barely changes.
The square temple, wide flat canopy and tiny central fitting match. The changed face of the entrance sits inside that same silhouette.
The classical and future temple have nearly identical roof edges, entry arch, central fixture and flanking supports. The facade pattern alone changes.
The industrial and future temples have the same roof slab, central fitting and wide entry. Small marks across the front do little to date the design.
The early well has an exposed horizontal winch beam between uprights. The classical well adds a substantial pitched canopy over the round shaft.
The early well's long exposed crossbeam becomes compact winch equipment with a tall offset upright. The large circular well remains recognizable.
The classical well wears a broad roof over the shaft. The open industrial well directly exposes a winch and a single high post.
Both arenas are the same open circular bowl interrupted by two bud-capped towers. The changed tower tips account for only a few pixels.
The open ring, stepped seating and two opposing bud towers remain in the same positions. The future tower still reads as the same bud.
The same paired bud towers rise above the same arena rim and seating. Their slightly different caps do little to establish a later age.
Both coal mines have the same peaked frame, sloping side braces and rounded annex. The industrial and future equipment are difficult to tell apart.
The round plot, grove of crops and bulb-shaped shed are the same from both sides. Small changes along the shed roof leave the early farms too similar.
Both farms have the same circular plot, rows and bulbous shed. The second small upright on the future farm is an incremental addition.
The iron mine's rounded rear chamber rises above a low headframe. The industrial headframe becomes a tall pointed truss with the chamber lower beside it.
The low arch forward of the iron mine chamber becomes a tall pointed lifting frame. The arcing braces now dominate the gold mine from both views.
The industrial and future mines repeat the tall pointed lifting frame, low annex and split braces. Their equipment and skyline almost coincide.
Both grain stores show three tightly clustered pods in the same hierarchy. Only their faceting and the tips of their caps change.
The grain pods remain clustered at the same heights. The industrial example sharpens their tops slightly while retaining the same footprint and main mass.
The future grain pods have sharper tips, but they still use the same three pods, proportions, arrangement and supporting base as the early store.
Both granaries use two taller pods and a short one in the same positions. The changed curvature around the caps is slight.
The three grain pods keep the same arrangement and proportions. Pointing their caps gives too little change to distinguish the future installation.
Both granaries are effectively the same cluster of pointed pods. The future caps are slightly longer with a seam down one pod.
The circular paddock, small shelter, troughs and low perimeter repeat. The altered peak on the shelter is small at this scale.
An extra small upright sits beside the shelter, but the same round paddock, troughs and hut still read as the same pasture.
The early paddock gains an upright and a more pointed shelter. Both views still show the same low ring, tiny hut and trough layout.
The circular paddock, shelter and troughs repeat. The industrial version adds a small upright by the hut without changing the overall working silhouette.
Both pastures show the same paddock and shelter. An upright beside the hut adds too little equipment or skyline to establish the future era.
Both pastures repeat their hut, outer ring and small upright. The later tip of the hut roof and upright barely change their contour.
The same stadium bowl, entry break and two tall sloping frame screens dominate both views. The small change at the top of a frame is easy to miss.
Both universities have a bud-capped cylindrical tower attached to an open curved court. The tower hood changes angle while the campus form repeats.
The same tall bud tower and low curved court dominate. The tower cap becomes a little asymmetric, with no other clear change at 64 pixels.
A slightly different slope on the tower cap is the principal visible change. The tower, court and front piers have the same mass and arrangement.
The early bank is a broad conical roof over a round vault. The industrial bank's roof flattens into a low drum visible between raised perimeter posts.
Both banks have a conical roof over the same round vault and entry. Extending the posts around the future roof leaves the dominant form alike.
The low, recessed industrial roof gives way to a rising cone framed by tall flanking posts. The round bank block and entry remain readable.
Both cathedrals have the same gabled nave between large capped entry turrets. The new ridge pinnacle is a small change above the same church.
The same tall, spiked coal headframe, attached hut and ore stockpile dominate. A flat cap takes the place of the small crown above the industrial frame.
The farmstead keeps its field rows, round hut and small store in the same positions. A taller, pointed cap on the classical hut barely changes the plot.
The field, clustered silos and round shed keep the same outline. The future shed roof and the ends of the silos change slightly.
The same round dock hut and landing project over the same boat gear. The industrial roof is a little flatter but the fishing operation repeats.
Both fishing huts have the same round cabin, platform and boat gear. The industrial hut rounds off the peak of the previous roof.
The foundry repeats its two stacks, squat furnace and free-standing equipment. Only the small secondary stack changes profile appreciably.
The same lifting frame rises from the same gold workings. The pointed crown changes into a flatter cap while the headgear retains the same proportion.
The ore pile, spiked headframe, hut and bins remain in position. Extra fittings in the industrial version sit inside that same mine outline.
The gold mine's peaked frame receives a wider slab cap. Its braces, low hut and ore cluster repeat, keeping the two installations too close.
The classical cap gives way to a spiked pulley head. The tall frame, shed and rock heap look much the same beneath it.
The two gold mine frames have the same roof, shaft and squat annex. A new small fitting beside the stockpile barely affects the profile.
Both mines retain the same spiked frame sides, gear pile and annex. The future slab cap is too small to distinguish a new installation.
Both hunting lodges show the same round tent and flanking drying rack. Small roof seam and entry changes leave the silhouette intact.
The military base repeats a single long hall and the same end tower. The extended tower and second roof finial provide limited separation.
The tower, four crossed sails, roof and attached hut are nearly identical. No substantial change to the orc mill's mechanism reads from either angle.
The extraction camp repeats its spiked frame, shed and rock piles. Changing the pinnacle to a small square cap leaves the same silhouette below.
Both mines share the same forked frame, drifts and low hut. A small industrial fitting beside the ore changes little at this size.
The future square cap sits above the same tall lifting frame, rock pile and entrance used on the early mine.
The small flat cap becomes a forked crown. The same lifting tower, rock field and end hut dominate the classical and industrial silhouettes.
Both mines have a slab-capped lifting frame and nearly identical low ore huts. The small fittings by the rocks do not establish a different age.
The slab cap and one small change by the ore are visible, but the industrial frame, entrance and pile arrangement otherwise repeat in the future mine.
Both pastures show the same central conical hut, rectangular pens and little troughs. Their slightly different roof tips are lost at thumbnail size.
The later hut has a lower cap, but it remains the same round shelter within the same pens and trough arrangement.
Taking the point off the hut roof produces a small change to the central silhouette. The low pen layout and working equipment remain alike.
The pronounced hut peak rounds off. Its base, the pens and the pasture equipment still occupy the same positions and scale.
The future pasture has the same round central hut and identical yard. Its blunter roof changes too little of the working silhouette.
Both pastures repeat the same low, rounded hut, rectangular paddock and equipment. A change at the top of the roof barely registers.
Both sawmills use a round-roof hut, parallel log stacks and the same low sawing bed. The small upright at the logs is the clearest change.
Both quarries have the same angled hoist over the cut and the same round hut alongside. A slight change to the hut peak leaves the operation identical.
The quarry face, pole frame, lifting beam and operator hut match closely. The industrial hut roof flattens a little.
The hoist and lower quarry cut retain the same outline. The hut loses a few pixels at its crown in the future version.
Both quarries repeat the same angular hoist, stair-like cut and small hut. The hut roof rounds off while the working equipment repeats.
The same crane and inclined working face dominate. A shorter cap on the hut changes too little to distinguish the future quarry.
The industrial and future quarries are nearly indistinguishable in both views, down to the hoist angle, rock placement and low hut.
Both weavers use the same large outward-leaning cloth rack beside a round hut. Its roof peak flattens, but the work and silhouette repeat.
The round hut, stockpiled trunks and chopping block repeat. The industrial version mainly adds a small fitting at the back of the logs.
The later woodcamp rounds off the hut roof and changes a small fitting at the log pile. Hut, logs and chopping block keep the same working arrangement.
The same broad, low canopy sits above an open workshop frame. Tiny fittings change on the roof and bench while its structural outline repeats.
The earlier bank has a broad sloping cap down to the entrance. The industrial bank has a raised, rounded vault roof with a strong horizontal ledge beneath it.
The low sloping roof above the early bank becomes a tall square upper storey with a flat crown over the familiar vault entrance.
The industrial bank's rounded raised roof gives way to a clearly square, stepped upper block. Both retain the stepped base, projecting entry and apex emblem.
The barracks retain the same two parallel roofs around an open entrance. A narrow crest on the classical ridge is the most visible change.
Both barracks retain the paired wings, center stair and front gate. The industrial pipe adds a small point to the same skyline.
The entrance and two long flanking quarters repeat. The later roof fittings are too small to distinguish the future barracks.
The central roof crest gives way to a pipe at one end. The barracks' two wings, gate and stairs keep nearly the same outline.
The same two quarters flank the same entry. The industrial chimney and the future group of short roof fittings differ too little at phone size.
The classical bath has a large domed steam room. A conspicuous tall exhaust stack rises over the lower industrial boiler roof beside the same baths.
Both coal mines show a tall lifting frame, adjacent low shed and ore piles. The widened cap adds only a few pixels at the top of the same headgear.

The square cap is wider on the classical headframe, but the same ore cut, braces, lifting frame and neighboring shed dominate these gold mines.

The small overhanging cap gives way to a narrower machinery head. The gold mine's adjacent cut, shaft and working platform repeat.

A ridge finial becomes a small stepped cap while the same roofs cover the same projecting stalls. The market operation reads alike.
The classical and future stalls share the same stocky canopies and front entry. Lowering the center ridge changes little at thumbnail size.
Both have the same low market wings and entry. The little raised central cap becomes a slightly wider inset panel.
Both extraction camps have the same narrow shaft, inclined cut and adjacent shelter. The classical shaft gains a wider cap.

The lifting frame trades its splayed cap for a narrower head. The shaft, ore yard and adjoining cut retain the same main outlines.
Both mines use the same projecting cap on the same narrow shaft. Raising the headframe above the cut changes its height rather than its operating structure.

Both shrines repeat the same open pavilion, altar, stairs and pyramidal roof. A minor change at the ridge hardly affects the outline.

The same four-post canopy and altar sit above identical stairs. A slight change in roof pitch is the clearest difference visible.

Both shrines show the same low roof, pillars, center altar and broad stairs. Only the outer edge of the future canopy appears slightly different.

The industrial temple's small solid emblem sits above a sloping cap. The future temple has a large open ring over a low rectangular sanctuary.

The iron center's low wide canopy gives way to a steep tall pyramid that occupies much more of the medieval tower's height above the terrace.
The little lantern above the Renaissance dome adds a few pixels of height, but the classical dome, square cornice and terraced hall repeat.
